implementation_notes: Default realization today: an enum (or final class) whose static storage holds the keys and a Dictionary of entries, with register/lookup static methods and a lock (NSLock or os_unfair_lock) around mutation. It replaces the Registry class with static members and keeps synchronous, non-async call sites; under strict concurrency the storage must be marked nonisolated(unsafe) (or the whole type be @MainActor), which is an explicit promise that the lock provides the safety.
pitfalls: Static storage is never released: every registered instance lives for the process lifetime, so a registry that holds view controllers, caches or observers leaks memory unless entries are removed explicitly.

An unchecked cast on lookup (as? T) turns a mistyped key into a runtime RegistryError/unknown-service at the call site rather than a compile error - keying by a generic type or protocol constraint removes most of that risk.
nonisolated(unsafe) only silences the compiler: the lock must cover every read and write, and re-entrant calls (a factory that registers) deadlock with a non-recursive lock.

variants.name: actor-isolated registry
variants.implementation_notes: Swift concurrency answer: an actor owns the dictionary, so register and lookup are isolated and serialized by the runtime and no manual lock is needed; lookup becomes async (await) and stored values must be Sendable. This is the recommended shape when registrations or lookups can arrive from concurrent tasks under Swift 6 strict concurrency, and it is the only variant where concurrent access is checked by the compiler.
pitfalls: Isolation makes access async: every call site needs await (or resolve sends into the actor), and accessing the registry from a synchronous context (initializers, property observers) is no longer possible without a Task detour.
Values stored in an actor must be Sendable; non-Sendable references (view controllers, reference-type plugins) need @unchecked Sendable wrappers or actor-local proxies.
An actor-isolated registry serializes every lookup, so a hot path pays actor-hop latency - within an actor, callers should receive the service once and cache it locally.
